DocumentationNarrative.Title: Models

DocumentationNarrative.Body:
A typical path can begin with a live system extracted into `MetaSchema`, then move through explicit data-type policy, vault or dimensional architecture, modeled and bound SQL transforms, generated database assets, data-quality review, pipeline execution, orchestration, and a portable `MetaAnalytics` model projected into Tabular or MultiDimensional form.
Teams compose the sanctioned workspaces that match their architecture. At every handoff, the input and output remain inspectable model instances instead of disappearing into generator configuration or unstructured deployment scripts.
DocumentationNarrative.Title: From source contracts to analytical targets

DocumentationNarrative.Body:
The architecture is also exercised as one complete system. The checked-in AdventureWorks stack composes 27 workspaces and 30 named operations over a live `AdventureWorks2022` source:
- synchronize the source schema into `MetaSchema`; - generate and deploy Raw and Business Data Vault structures and a dimensional warehouse; - import and strictly bind 53 source-to-Raw, 47 Raw-to-Business, and 20 Business-to-warehouse transforms; - author three pipelines and infer their cross-pipeline orchestration from modeled task and binding evidence; - generate and deploy 176 Data Quality checks; - author portable `MetaAnalytics` semantics, project them into `MetaTabular`, then deploy and process the model.
A clean run reconciled 31,465 orders, 121,317 order lines, and 163 quota rows from source through the warehouse. It reproduced total due `123216786.1159`, line sales `109846381.4250`, quota `95714000.0000`, and zero findings across the promoted Data Quality checks. Repeating the complete ETL preserved the modeled Raw, Business, and warehouse row totals. A processed Tabular deployment returned the same analytical values.
After the named create and deploy operations have materialized the stack, execution remains concise:
```powershell cd Demos\AdventureWorksBiStackDemo\AdventureWorksBiStackDemo.MetaMesh meta-mesh operations meta-mesh run --operation run-etl meta-mesh run --operation verify-stack meta-mesh run --operation deploy-tabular meta-mesh run --operation process-tabular ```
The demo README records the complete build order, local services, environment variables, layer-by-layer execution options, and cleanup operation.
DocumentationNarrative.Title: A complete stack in practice

DocumentationNarrative.Body:
The sanctioned models divide BI concerns at their natural ownership boundaries:
- **Source and type contracts:** `MetaSchema` captures systems, schemas, tables, fields, keys, and relationships from SQL Server. `MetaDataType` and `MetaDataTypeConversion` carry semantic types and explicit mappings into runtime type systems. - **Data architecture:** `MetaRawDataVault` and `MetaBusinessDataVault` model raw and governed vault structures. `MetaDataWarehouse` models dimensions, facts, grain, business keys, roles, snapshots, bridges, and slowly changing dimensions. Separate implementation workspaces own physical SQL naming, keys, platform columns, defaults, and indexes. - **Transform and database realization:** `MetaTransformScript`, `MetaTransformBinding`, `MetaSql`, and `MetaSqlDeployManifest` carry understood SQL, schema contracts, deployable objects, and controlled deployment. - **Analytical semantics:** `MetaAnalytics` defines portable tables, attributes, hierarchies, measures, aggregation behavior, relationships, perspectives, roles, cultures, and translations before an engine is selected. - **Analytical targets:** `MetaTabular` owns DAX measures, calculation groups, partitions, KPIs, and tabular security. `MetaMultiDimensional` owns cubes, measure groups, MDX, named sets, actions, partitions, and multidimensional security. - **Execution and assurance:** `MetaDataQuality`, `MetaPipeline`, and `MetaOrchestration` turn modeled transform and access evidence into reviewable checks, executable task chains, dependency graphs, synchronization policy, and runtime evidence.
`meta-convert` performs explicit conversions between sanctioned model surfaces, keeping portable intent separate from target-specific implementation details.
DocumentationNarrative.Title: Sanctioned model layers

DocumentationNarrative.Body:
The runtime tools consume modeled evidence produced by the layers before them:
- **`meta-data-quality`** traverses the typed transform graph to discover reviewable integrity, optionality, fanout, duplicate, join-pattern, and filter-consensus candidates. Binding evidence can restrict generation to transforms whose source and target contracts are already proven. - **`meta-pipeline`** executes modeled transform-backed and external-process tasks, records the exact transform and binding used, and preserves row, batch, timeout, fingerprint, audit, and failure evidence. - **`meta-orchestration`** derives the provable dependency graph from pipeline tasks and bound object reads and writes. Explicit ordering, lock compatibility, synchronization, and failure branches remain modeled policy instead of being buried in scheduler behavior. - **Target CLIs** realize modeled SQL, Tabular, and MultiDimensional workspaces through deployment and processing commands owned by the target model.
Automation therefore follows from explicit contracts. When additional knowledge is required, it enters as modeled policy that engineers and agents can inspect alongside the inferred evidence.
DocumentationNarrative.Title: Model-driven execution and evidence

DocumentationNarrative.Body:
SQL is represented as structure rather than carried as an opaque script blob.
- **`MetaTransformScript`** imports the supported T-SQL surface into a typed syntax graph covering statement roots, query composition, joins, expressions, predicates, grouping, windowing, functions, and bounded mutation statements. The model emits semantically equivalent SQL and proves stability through `SQL -> workspace -> SQL -> workspace` round trips. - **`MetaTransformBinding`** resolves modeled source and target identifiers against explicit `MetaSchema` workspaces. It records rowsets, columns, source objects, target objects, and validation links, and checks target shape and data-type compatibility through sanctioned `MetaDataTypeConversion` policy. - **`MetaSql`** carries deployable database structure, while `MetaSqlDeployManifest` makes source and live fingerprints, schema changes, destructive approvals, and deployment actions explicit before execution.
That shared understanding lets later layers reason from transform structure and binding evidence instead of reparsing SQL independently or guessing from text.
DocumentationNarrative.Title: SQL as modeled structure

DocumentationNarrative.Body: `meta-bi` is a model-driven BI engineering stack built on the generic `meta` foundation. It keeps source structures, SQL semantics, transformation contracts, data architecture, deployment assets, execution plans, and analytical targets as typed workspaces that can be inspected, converted, generated, and executed through one model-first foundation.

DocumentationNarrative.Body:
`meta` follows the working lifecycle of a metadata workspace:
- **Create and inspect:** initialize workspaces and inspect their current model and instance state (`init`, `status`). - **Explore:** list, view, query, and traverse modeled data (`list`, `view`, `query`, `graph`). - **Author:** change model definitions and instance data through model-aware commands (`model ...`, `insert`, `delete`, `bulk-insert`, `instance ...`). - **Refactor:** analyze candidate relationships and apply atomic model-plus-instance changes (`model suggest`, `model refactor ...`). - **Exchange representations:** import source material and generate SQL, C#, and other sanctioned consumables (`import ...`, `generate ...`).
A typical flow starts with a model and instance workspace, uses `meta` to preserve and transform that modeled truth, then emits the native artifacts needed by databases, applications, and downstream generators.
DocumentationNarrative.Title: Meta CLI at a glance

DocumentationNarrative.Body:
Workspace-oriented commands use the **current working directory** when `--workspace` is omitted. They do not search parent directories. Use `--workspace <path>` when the target workspace is elsewhere.
Common command behavior:
- successful state changes print `Ok`; - usage and runtime failures explain what prevented the command from continuing and return a non-zero exit code; - mutating commands that expose `--strict` promote warnings to errors.
**Discover the command surface**
```powershell meta help meta help model meta model suggest --help ```
Top-level help lists command groups. Command help then narrows the surface to the relevant usage, arguments, and options.
DocumentationNarrative.Title: Command guide

DocumentationNarrative.Body:
Create a workspace, add a small model and one row, then emit SQL and C# outputs from the same model and instance graph.
```powershell meta init .\Workspace cd .\Workspace meta model rename-model MetadataModel WorkspaceCatalog meta model add-entity System meta model add-property System SystemName --required true meta insert System 1 --set "SystemName=Enterprise Analytics Platform" meta status meta generate sql --out ..\out\sql meta generate csharp --out ..\out\csharp --tooling ```
DocumentationNarrative.Title: Create a workspace and emit SQL/C#
One sample across XML, SQL, and C#

DocumentationNarrative.Body:
In this project, metadata is not an annotation around the product. **Metadata is the product model itself.**
- **`model.xml`** declares the schema contract: entities, scalar properties, and relationships. - **`instances/*.xml`** carries the instance graph for that model: records, values, and relationship usages. - **`workspace.xml`** records workspace-level representation and storage configuration.
Core terms:
- **Model:** a named set of entity definitions. - **Entity:** a record type, comparable to a table or a POCO type. - **Property:** a scalar attribute on an entity instance. - **Relationship:** a modeled reference from one entity to another. - **Instance:** one identified record of an entity. - **Workspace:** an on-disk unit containing a model, its instances, and workspace configuration.
DocumentationNarrative.Title: Metadata foundations

DocumentationNarrative.Body:
Build the foundation and weave solutions with .NET 8:
```powershell dotnet build Metadata.Framework.sln dotnet build MetaWeave.sln ```
Run a CLI directly from its project during development:
```powershell dotnet run --project Meta/Cli/Meta.Cli.csproj -- help ```
When the CLI output directory is on `PATH`, use the executable name directly:
```powershell meta help ```
On Windows, the `meta`, `meta-weave`, and `meta-docs` project builds also refresh their framework-dependent publish directories under `Cli\bin\publish\win-x64`.
Build the offline installer package with:
```powershell powershell -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File Meta\Installer\package-offline.ps1 ```
The default package is framework-dependent and requires the .NET 8 runtime on the target machine. Use `-SelfContained` only when the package must carry its own runtime.
Install the packaged `meta`, `meta-weave`, and `meta-docs` CLIs into `%LOCALAPPDATA%\meta\bin` with:
```powershell Meta\Installer\bin\publish\win-x64-framework-dependent-shared\install-meta.exe ```
DocumentationNarrative.Title: Install and run

DocumentationNarrative.Body:
`instances/*.xml` carries the data for a model.
- The document root is the model name, such as `<EnterpriseBIPlatform>`. - Each entity's records appear under a deterministic list container such as `<CubeList>` or `<MeasureList>`. - Each record uses the singular entity name and has an `Id="..."` attribute. - Relationship usages are stored as `...Id` attributes. A relationship to `Cube` becomes `CubeId`; a relationship with `role="SourceCube"` becomes `SourceCubeId`. - Scalar properties are child elements. A missing element is unset; an empty element is an explicitly empty string.
These XML conventions are deterministic representation rules. The loaded C# model still carries relationships as object references, while generated SQL carries them as relational keys.
DocumentationNarrative.Title: Instance XML contract

DocumentationNarrative.Body:
The foundation libraries are available as internal NuGet packages:
- `Meta.Core` - `Meta.Adapters` - `MetaWeave.Core`
Build them into the local `.nupkg` feed with:
```powershell .\pack-internal.cmd ```
Downstream repositories consume packages rather than project references back into this repository. That keeps the foundation boundary explicit and prevents downstream changes from silently reaching into core source.
`meta-bi` currently consumes `Meta.Core` from this feed. `MetaWeave.Core` is published alongside it for consumers that need sanctioned cross-model binding services.
DocumentationNarrative.Title: Internal packages

DocumentationNarrative.Body:
Isomorphic metadata preserves the **same structure and meaning** across its supported representations instead of translating each representation into a different product model.
One model can therefore have three native working surfaces, each suited to a different kind of work:
- **XML workspace:** deterministic, reviewable, and git-friendly for authoring and version control. - **SQL:** relational and database-native, with keys and constraints carrying integrity where data platforms already work. - **C#:** application-native, with strongly typed objects and object references for tools, services, and generated consumers.
Because the semantics remain aligned, different producers and consumers can collaborate without rebuilding the model at every boundary:
- analysts and modelers can author and review workspace data; - platform engineers can consume SQL and SQL-project outputs; - application and tooling engineers can consume generated C# APIs.
DocumentationNarrative.Title: Why isomorphic metadata

DocumentationNarrative.Body:
`model.xml` declares the schema of a metadata workspace: which entities exist, which scalar properties they carry, and how they relate.
A model has one `<Model name=...>` root and follows a small set of rules:
- `<Entity name=Cube>` defines a record type; every entity has an implicit `Id`. - `<PropertyList>` contains scalar text fields. Properties are required by default, and `isRequired=false` makes a property optional. - `<RelationshipList>` contains references to other entities. Relationships are required by default. - A relationship role is used when more than one relationship targets the same entity and the references need distinct meanings. - XML instance containers and generated C# root collections use the deterministic `<EntityName>List` convention.
The model contract is intentionally small. Meaning that must survive generation belongs in entities, properties, and relationships rather than in parser conventions or surrounding prose.
DocumentationNarrative.Title: Model XML contract

DocumentationNarrative.Body:
The foundation is delivered through five command-line tools:
- **`meta`** authors and transforms model and instance workspaces, performs model-aware inspection and refactoring, imports external representations, and generates SQL and C# consumables. - **`meta-cli`** models command grammars and supplies the shared parser, help, workspace-loading, and handler runtime used by the suite. - **`meta-weave`** defines and validates sanctioned property bindings across models, then materializes those bindings when one combined workspace is needed. - **`meta-docs`** combines generated reference facts with authored technical documentation, then merges and renders the public reference. - **`meta-mesh`** declares the workspaces involved in a repository workflow and the ordered executable steps that operate on them.
BI-specific sanctioned models and command-line tools live in the separate `meta-bi` repository.
DocumentationNarrative.Title: Foundation command-line tools

DocumentationNarrative.Body: `meta` is a deterministic metadata backend for defining structured models once and carrying them across XML, SQL, and C# without semantic drift. XML workspaces provide a git-friendly authoring surface, while generated SQL and C# provide native relational and application surfaces over the same model and instance graph.

DocumentationNarrative.Body:
MetaAnalytics is the portable semantic model of the BI stack. It describes data sources, tables, attributes, hierarchies, measures, facts, relationships, and security in a target-neutral form that architects and analysts can review before an analytical engine is chosen.
Analytical intent is explicit. A measure has a source and aggregation behavior, a hierarchy has a declared path, a table has a modeled purpose, and security belongs to the semantic model rather than being appended to a generated target. The result is a compact but expressive description of how the business should explore and calculate over the warehouse.
MetaConvert can project the same semantic contract into Tabular or MultiDimensional workspaces. Those target models add platform-specific capabilities while retaining the analytical design that the team agreed on here.

Start with a MetaCli workspace, add a command, mark it executable, then add the options the runtime should parse and document.
```powershell meta-cli new-workspace .\my-cli.MetaCli --application app-my-cli --standard-cli-shapes --default-help meta-cli add-command --workspace .\my-cli.MetaCli --id cmd-show --application app-my-cli --name show --token show --description "Show the workspace." meta-cli add-executable-command --workspace .\my-cli.MetaCli --id exec-show --command cmd-show meta-cli add-option --workspace .\my-cli.MetaCli --parameter-id param-show-workspace --option-id option-show-workspace --executable-command exec-show --name workspace --value-shape shape-path --token-id token-show-workspace --token --workspace --description "Workspace path." ```
DocumentationNarrative.Title: Create a small command surface

DocumentationNarrative.Body:
MetaCli is the modeled command-surface language used by the meta tools. An authored workspace describes an application, its command hierarchy, executable commands, parameters, option tokens, positional arguments, value shapes, allowed values, and parameter choices as ordinary model data.
That workspace is the source for shared parsing, help generation, runtime invocation, and documentation import. A command handler binds to an executable-command identity, while the runtime resolves modeled arguments and supplies the resulting invocation. Help and usage therefore come from the same surface that the parser accepts, rather than from a separate handwritten catalog.
The authoring CLI is intentionally precise. It makes the public grammar visible before behavior is attached, so a tool can be reviewed as a command-line product in its own right and then reused consistently by people, agents, documentation, and runtime code.

DocumentationNarrative.Body:
MetaConvert is the projection boundary between sanctioned BI workspaces. It carries an explicit source design into the next representation: source schema into raw vault, vault or warehouse into deployable SQL, quality evidence into SQL assets, or portable analytics into Tabular and MultiDimensional targets.
Every conversion starts from modeled inputs and produces a modeled output. Where a physical implementation or deployment policy is needed, that workspace is passed explicitly, keeping logical intent separate from target-specific choices. The converter therefore preserves a reviewable chain from source contract to generated artifact.
This makes the suite composable. A team can inspect each model in its own domain, regenerate a later projection when an upstream decision changes, and avoid treating an emitted script or target project as the place where the architecture is defined.

DocumentationNarrative.Body:
Generate review candidates from validated transforms, then promote approved candidates.
The binding workspace limits discovery to scripts whose source and target contracts are known. Promotion marks the candidates that should become generated SQL assets.
```powershell meta-data-quality from-transform-workspace --transform-workspace .\Transforms.Workspace --binding-workspace .\Binding.Workspace --new-workspace .\DataQuality.Workspace meta-data-quality inspect --workspace .\DataQuality.Workspace meta-data-quality promote --workspace .\DataQuality.Workspace --all meta-convert data-quality-to-sql --workspace .\DataQuality.Workspace --out .\DataQuality.sql ```
DocumentationNarrative.Title: Derive and promote quality evidence

DocumentationNarrative.Body:
MetaDataQuality derives reviewable quality candidates from typed transform and schema evidence. It examines the modeled transform graph, binding evidence, joins, relationships, and corpus patterns to identify missing references, uniqueness problems, unexpected null behavior, suspicious joins, and drift from repeated behavior.
Discovery is automatic because the technical basis is already modeled. Promotion remains deliberate: candidates become executable or review-oriented assets only when a user chooses to make that decision part of the workspace. The candidate, its evidence, and its promotion state stay together as inspectable data.
Generated SQL distinguishes runtime checks from semantic review findings. The resulting views and operational objects therefore preserve the reason a finding exists, support repeated execution, and give reviewers a clear route from a dashboard result back to the transform and schema evidence that produced it.

DocumentationNarrative.Body:
MetaDataTypeConversion records the sanctioned paths between declared data types. A conversion states the source and target systems together with the length, precision, scale, fallback, and compatibility behavior that determine whether a value can move across a boundary.
The conversion workspace is shared policy. Transform binding uses it to evaluate source-to-target compatibility, and generators can apply the same approved behavior when they project a model into SQL or another platform. This avoids quietly embedding widening assumptions in individual tools.
Keeping conversion rules modeled also makes the hard cases visible. A design can be reviewed for loss, truncation, precision, and fallback choices before a transform or target is generated, and the resulting decision is reusable wherever the same type boundary appears.

DocumentationNarrative.Body:
MetaDataType is the sanctioned vocabulary for types used throughout the modeled stack. A type catalog turns platform names, parameters, and identity behavior into reusable declarations instead of repeating those choices as loose strings in every schema, transform, and target.
The catalog gives downstream models a stable language for saying what a field or expression represents. Schema extraction, transform binding, warehouse design, analytics, and generated SQL can refer to the same declared type while each projection uses the natural syntax of its own platform.
That common vocabulary becomes especially valuable when a solution crosses SQL Server, analytical engines, and generated code. Type decisions stay inspectable at the model layer and conversion policy can build on them without inventing private compatibility rules.

DocumentationNarrative.Body:
A MetaMesh workspace names the workspaces that participate in repository work and records executable operations over them. Each declared workspace has one representation: an XML workspace path, a C# workspace path, or a SQL connection environment variable. Operations remain independent of that representation and invoke the product CLI that owns each domain action.
An operation contains an ordered chain of steps. Workspace tokens let those steps refer to declared inputs without embedding machine-specific paths. Environment tokens make external configuration explicit while keeping connection strings and other values out of the mesh. Before execution begins, MetaMesh resolves the workspaces used by the operation, executable lookup, working-directory access, and required environment variables.
Documentation regeneration, integration demos, and multi-workspace builds can therefore be inspected, validated, and replayed from the same model. Progress and failures identify the active step while each product CLI continues to own its behavior.
The AdventureWorks full-stack mesh uses this structure at system scale. Its operations synchronize a source schema, build and deploy Data Vault and warehouse layers, bind transforms, author pipelines, infer orchestration, generate Data Quality assets, and deploy a processed Tabular model.

DocumentationNarrative.Body:
Build orchestration from a modeled pipeline, then review the issues and plan.
Inference creates the provable part of the run graph. Any remaining ordering or lock decision is visible in the orchestration workspace before execution.
```powershell meta-orchestration infer --pipeline-workspace .\Pipeline.Workspace --new-workspace .\Orchestration.Workspace meta-orchestration list-issues --workspace .\Orchestration.Workspace meta-orchestration refresh-run-plan --workspace .\Orchestration.Workspace meta-orchestration inspect-run-plan --workspace .\Orchestration.Workspace ```
DocumentationNarrative.Title: Infer and review a run plan

DocumentationNarrative.Body:
MetaOrchestration turns modeled pipeline tasks and bound transform access evidence into a run graph. It derives the ordering that can be proven from declared reads, writes, and effects, then represents the remaining synchronization choices as explicit policy.
That division is deliberate. Structural evidence can establish a large portion of a safe plan, while dependency rules, lock policies, and concurrent-append decisions supply the operational knowledge that only a designer can provide. The resulting workspace makes both the inferred and authored portions of orchestration visible.
Execution coordinates the modeled run plan and retains run evidence. When an issue remains unresolved, it is recorded as a specific modeled concern rather than disappearing into scheduler code or an implicit ordering convention.

DocumentationNarrative.Body:
MetaPipeline models executable work as named pipelines and tasks. A task can be backed by a validated transform or by an explicit executable, with declared dependencies, connection context, timeouts, fingerprints, and the evidence needed to understand each run.
The workspace is the plan. It describes what should be executed and the contracts it relies on. The optional operational database records diagnostics, metrics, audits, and failures, giving an execution a useful history without becoming the source of model truth.

DocumentationNarrative.Title: Extract a source contract

DocumentationNarrative.Body:
MetaSchema captures a live source schema as an explicit workspace. The extracted model preserves the database and system context together with schemas, tables, fields, keys, and relationships, giving every later stage a reviewable source contract.
Extraction begins from the actual SQL Server surface and lets a team choose the schemas and tables that belong in the modeled boundary. The workspace records what the source exposes with enough structure for binding, conversion, vault design, warehouse design, and contract validation to reason about it directly.
Because the schema is durable model data, it can be compared, regenerated, and cited by downstream workspaces. A transform binds to this contract; a vault or warehouse derives from it; a deployment or quality check can state exactly which source objects it relies on.

DocumentationNarrative.Body:
Bind transform scripts to explicit source and target schemas.
Binding records the resolved source and target evidence only when every required reference and type rule can be proven from the supplied workspaces.
```powershell meta-transform-binding bind --transform-workspace .\Transforms.Workspace --source-schema .\SourceSchema.Workspace --target-schema .\WarehouseSchema.Workspace --execute-system SourceWarehouse --execute-system-default-schema-name dbo --new-workspace .\Binding.Workspace ```
DocumentationNarrative.Title: Validate a transform contract

DocumentationNarrative.Body:
MetaTransformBinding validates transform scripts against explicit source and target MetaSchema contracts. It resolves referenced objects and columns, verifies target write shape, evaluates data-type compatibility through the sanctioned conversion workspace, and records the resulting evidence in a dedicated binding workspace.
A successful binding says more than that the SQL parsed. It establishes that each modeled source and target reference resolves against the stated schemas and that the transform's write contract is compatible with its target. The recorded rowsets, columns, and validation links become a durable technical basis for later pipeline, orchestration, and quality work.
Strict mutation binding preserves the resolved reads and effects of `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `MERGE`, `DELETE`, and `TRUNCATE` statements. Its bounded expression analysis carries data types and nullability through direct columns, literals, parentheses, explicit `CAST` and `CONVERT`, compatible `CASE` and `COALESCE` expressions, and conjunctive `WHERE ... IS NOT NULL` evidence. Proven nullable writes to non-null targets fail; unknown evidence remains unknown rather than being invented.
Binding is an atomic contract gate in normal operation. Its explicit partial mode is for corpus discovery: it keeps the successfully bound scripts while preserving a report of the scripts that need more source, target, or type information.
DocumentationNarrative.Title: Working with MetaTransformBinding

The workspace captures the view structure once. Exported SQL can be compared with the source artifact or bound to an explicit schema contract.
```powershell meta-transform-script from sql-file --path .\views\v_customer.sql --new-workspace .\Transforms.Workspace --target dbo.v_customer meta-transform-script to sql-path --workspace .\Transforms.Workspace --out .\RoundTrippedSql ```

DocumentationNarrative.Body:
MetaTransformScript understands the supported SQL Server transform surface structurally. It imports views, query expressions, bounded mutation statements, inline table-valued functions, and constrained scalar functions into a typed workspace, then emits semantically equivalent SQL.
The workspace captures the parts of SQL that downstream tools need to reason about: statement ownership, identifiers, expressions, joins, common table expressions, predicates, grouping, windowing, type references, and source paths. A transform can therefore be inspected, bound to schemas, compared after a round-trip, and used as evidence by pipeline, orchestration, and data-quality tools.
The target is faithful syntax modeling. SQL is represented once as structured data, not reduced to a blob or replaced by a guessed lineage graph. Dynamic and procedural forms remain clearly bounded, while the supported surface can be proven through SQL-to-model-to-SQL equivalence and workspace diff evidence.

DocumentationNarrative.Body:

Evidence-backed suggestions help discover strong candidates, but the persisted binding remains an intentional modeled decision. Validation proves that every declared source value resolves through the binding it claims to use.
A valid weave can materialize a composed workspace when a consumer needs one model boundary. The weave itself remains the durable explanation of why that composition is correct and which source fields establish each cross-model link.

Use instance diff when two branches or workspaces evolved independently and you want a deterministic artifact describing the right-hand workspace changes.
```powershell meta instance diff .\BaselineWorkspace .\FeatureWorkspace meta instance merge .\IntegrationWorkspace .\FeatureWorkspace.instance-diff ```
DocumentationNarrative.Title: Move instance changes between workspaces

DocumentationNarrative.Body:
Workspaces evolve independently on different branches. `meta instance diff` and `meta instance merge` are deterministic synchronization primitives for instance data:
- `diff` produces a structured change artifact from Left -> Right. - `merge` applies that artifact to a target workspace with strict validation.
This is not a text diff. It is a semantic diff over entity rows, scalar values, and relationship usages.
Inputs:
- Left workspace - Right workspace
Output:
- a deterministic diff workspace artifact (default sibling path: `<RightWorkspace>.instance-diff`)
Mechanics:
- requires byte-identical `model.xml` for equal-model diff. - compares row identity by entity + `Id`. - compares scalar property values. - compares relationship usage values (`...Id` attributes). - compares row presence/absence.
Conceptual change classes captured by the artifact:
- added rows (present in Right, absent in Left) - removed rows (present in Left, absent in Right) - updated scalar values on shared rows - updated relationship references on shared rows
Determinism guarantees:
- canonical ordering/normalization is applied before writing the diff artifact. - entity/property traversal and row comparisons are stable. - same inputs produce the same logical diff artifact.
The artifact is a structured description of how to transform Left into Right.
DocumentationNarrative.Title: What instance diff does

DocumentationNarrative.Body: Apply an aligned instance diff artifact to a target workspace.
DocumentationNarrative.Title: Summary

DocumentationNarrative.Body:
`meta instance diff` and `meta instance merge` are not:
- text merge tools. - automatic conflict resolution. - model/schema merge. - record matching by business key. - best-effort partial reconciliation.
DocumentationNarrative.Title: What this is not

DocumentationNarrative.Body:
Merge is strict. It fails rather than writing invalid state.
- required relationship usage missing -> validation failure. - relationship target row missing -> validation failure. - deleting rows that remain referenced -> validation failure. - relationship updates are applied as part of the snapshot and validated with the whole workspace.
Operation ordering is snapshot-based: merge builds the target end state in memory, validates, then saves. It does not persist partial intermediate steps.
Rows are matched by identity (`Entity`, `Id`), not by value similarity.
- identity stability is assumed. - no fuzzy matching. - no business-key reconciliation. - if a target workspace has drifted so that an incoming `Id` would collide with different state, merge fails its precondition instead of remapping or guessing.
DocumentationNarrative.Title: Referential integrity and row identity

DocumentationNarrative.Body:
Inputs:
- target workspace - diff artifact workspace (from `meta instance diff`)
Operation:
- verifies precondition: target must match the diff Left snapshot. - applies the diff Right snapshot to the target in memory. - normalizes and validates the resulting workspace. - persists once only if validation/postconditions pass.
Atomicity and safety:
- all changes are applied or none are persisted. - any failure restores pre-merge in-memory state and aborts. - save is a single workspace write operation after successful validation. - rows created by merge keep the `Id` values recorded in the diff artifact. - merge never allocates replacement ids or remaps existing ids.
Determinism:
- same target + same diff artifact -> same resulting workspace state.
DocumentationNarrative.Title: What instance merge does

DocumentationNarrative.Body: Apply a structured instance diff to a target workspace only when its precondition still matches, so workspace changes synchronize without text merges.
DocumentationNarrative.Title: Summary

DocumentationNarrative.Body:
Example flow with two independently evolved workspaces:
1. baseline/integration workspace is your Left reference. 2. feature workspace with intended changes is your Right reference. 3. generate diff from Left -> Right. 4. apply diff into integration target (which must still match Left snapshot).
`meta instance diff .\WorkspaceA .\WorkspaceB` `meta instance merge .\WorkspaceA .\WorkspaceB.instance-diff`
If merge precondition fails, regenerate diff against the current target baseline.
`model refactor property-to-relationship` changes instance structure (scalar values moved to required relationship usages). Diff/merge captures and replays those instance-level structural value changes when both sides share the same model contract.
For model-contract drift between workspaces, use the aligned diff/merge path (`instance diff-aligned` / `instance merge-aligned`) with explicit alignment mappings.

DocumentationNarrative.Body:
This is the intended landing workflow: import flat CSVs with stable row Ids, run suggest, then apply an atomic model+instance refactor.
`meta model suggest` is structural and deterministic. It prints strong exact-name relationship promotions by default and prints weak suggestions separately when RI is still complete but the target is only a role-style suffix match or the same source property matches more than one eligible target.
Eligible means the promotion satisfies 100% referential integrity (RI) before any mutation:
- source lands first as a scalar `...Id` field (for example `WarehouseId`) - target lookup property is complete and unambiguous (no null/blank values, no duplicates) - source property is complete (no null/blank values) - every source value resolves to an existing target lookup value (full coverage, no unmatched values) - source and target scalar types are compatible under strict rules (no implicit casting) - source values are reused, so the source behaves like a reference and the direction is structurally evidenced as many-to-one
For Id-first landing, the sanctioned structural rule is `ProductId -> Product.Id`, `SupplierId -> Supplier.Id`, and so on. `meta model suggest` does not rely on `Code` fields for this workflow. If any rule fails, the item is not printed.

DocumentationNarrative.Body:
Meta is the foundation tool for creating, evolving, inspecting, and projecting typed metadata workspaces. A workspace declares a model and its instance graph once, then makes that same structure available as deterministic XML, relational SQL, and typed C# without changing its meaning.
The CLI owns the everyday lifecycle: initialize a workspace, inspect its model and rows, make intentional edits, import a source surface, and generate a consumable representation. Model refactors rewrite the corresponding instance structure atomically, while structured diff and merge preserve stable row identities so workspace evolution can participate in normal code review and branch workflows.
The result is a durable model boundary. A database, generator, service, or analytical tool can consume a natural representation for its environment while staying connected to the same declared entities, properties, relationships, and data.
